# Real background execution

Bash and Agent now accept `run_in_background: true`. They return JSON with a
`task_id` and initial `status`. TaskGet/TaskList expose the same task, and TaskOutput
returns its current status, bounded output and (for Bash) exit code. Set
`block: true` with `timeout` to wait up to 600000 ms; a wait timeout does not cancel
the task. `TaskStop` requests real cancellation. `agent.stopTask(id)` waits for the
owned execution to settle. All task lookup and cancellation are session-scoped.

```ts
// Tool inputs generated by the model:
// Bash:       { command: "npm test", run_in_background: true }
// TaskOutput: { id: "<returned task_id>", block: true, timeout: 30000 }
// TaskStop:   { id: "<returned task_id>" }
```

Background work is scoped to the QueryEngine invocation that created it. It runs
alongside subsequent model turns. On normal completion the engine joins its work,
emits `system/task_notification` events, and then reports the final result with all
child usage included. Each notification reports the task's own terminal status;
the parent result describes the parent run, not whether every child succeeded.
Consumers must check both. On interruption, exhausted turns/budget, failure or an
early iterator exit, owned background work is cancelled and joined. Goal rounds
therefore do not leave work running into the next round. This is not a daemon or a
cross-query job service, and resumed transcripts do not restart background work.

Bash captures stdout/stderr as they arrive, retains a bounded output tail (100000
characters), and reports nonzero exits, timeout and cancellation as errors. On
POSIX systems commands have a process group: cancellation sends SIGTERM to that
group and escalates to SIGKILL after 500 ms. Processes that intentionally detach into
a new session are outside that group. Windows currently cancels only the direct
process; full Windows process-tree management is not implemented. Child stdin is
closed; interactive terminals remain outside this API.

Background subagents inherit the parent's provider, tool and permission constraints,
shared budget and cancellation. Their output is available on completion. Custom
providers and tools must cooperate with AbortSignal; the SDK cannot forcefully
terminate arbitrary JavaScript callbacks. Parallel requests can overshoot the
admission-based cost cap, as documented in the runtime reliability notes.

TaskCreate continues to create tracking records. TaskUpdate cannot overwrite runtime
status or output for real executions. Cancellation is a request until the execution
settles; TaskOutput can wait for that transition. Direct tool callers that bypass
Agent/QueryEngine own cleanup and must stop their tasks explicitly.

## Capability honesty

The catalog still contains 35 base tool definitions. CronCreate/CronDelete/CronList
and RemoteTrigger are disabled and excluded from model schemas because no scheduler
or remote backend is installed. Other conditional tools such as Skill may further
reduce the available set. Direct cron helpers manage definitions only; they do not
schedule execution. RemoteTrigger reports an error when called directly. LSP's
advertised description now explicitly identifies its lexical search fallback.
A real scheduler, language-server integration and search backend remain separate
follow-up work.

## Verification

Offline tests cover actual Bash output and nonzero exits, timeouts, cancellation
including TERM-resistant process groups, bounded output, session isolation, runtime
status protection, subagent cancellation, shared usage at completion, iterator
cleanup and suppression of disabled tool schemas. No paid model API is used.
